# Anupada Sutta (MN 111 (PTS MN iii 25))
**ID:** MN 111 (PTS MN iii 25)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Anupada Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** One by One
**PTS:** MN iii 25
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn111

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Anupada Sutta* ("One by One", MN 111) is a discourse set in the *Majjhimanikāya* (PTS MN iii 25–29) in which the Buddha praises the wisdom of Venerable Sāriputta and describes in technical detail his practice of insight into mental phenomena one by one as they occurred (*anupadadhamma-vipassanā*) [SuttaCentral; Emmanuel 2013; Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. The sutta recounts Sāriputta's two-week period of striving after ordination, detailing how he attained mastery (*vasippatta*) and perfection (*pāramippatta*) across the nine meditative attainments—the four fine-material absorptions (*jhāna*s), the four immaterial attainments, and the cessation of perception and feeling [Endo 1997; Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. Upon emerging from each of the first seven states, Sāriputta introspectively identified and investigated their constituent mental factors (such as contact, feeling, perception, volition, consciousness, zeal, decision, energy, mindfulness, equanimity, and attention) as they arose, remained, and passed away [Nyanaponika and Bodhi 2012; Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Qian Lin 2015].
Scholars widely observe that the sutta's extensive classification of mental constituents anticipates the Abhidhamma method and the development of the *cetasika* category [SuttaCentral; Dhammajoti 2007; Emmanuel 2013; Nyanaponika and Bodhi 2012]. C. A. F. Rhys Davids questioned the authenticity of the sutta, arguing that it represents an editorial patchwork composed long after Sāriputta's death [Nyanaponika and Bodhi 2012]. Anālayo also points to indicators of later influence, noting the presence of internal inconsistencies in the factor lists and the term *anupadavavatthita* ("one by one determination"), an expression uncharacteristic of early discourses and found primarily in later texts [Anālayo 2014].
Text-reuse analysis by DharmaNexus reflects shared stock phrasing with canonical and post-canonical Pali works, including the *Theragāthā-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Niddesa* treatises (*Khaggavisāṇa-*, *Tuvaṭaka-*, and *Purābhedasuttaniddesa*), the *Aṅguttaranikāya* (AN 4 and AN 9), and the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, as well as automatic formulaic segment alignments with the Chinese *Madhyama-āgama* (T 26) and Tibetan *Prajñāpāramitā* corpora [DharmaNexus].

- [Nyanaponika et al. 2003] Nyanaponika Thera, Hellmuth Hecker, and Bhikkhu Bodhi, Great Disciples of the Buddha: Their Lives, Their Works, Their Legacy (2003) — Account of Sāriputta's two-week practice of anupadadhamma-vipassanā across the nine meditative attainments.
